name: Vetiver

card.summary: An earthy, smoky grass-root oil used as a base note and fixative in colognes, giving men's fragrances a dry, woody character that makes the scent last longer on skin.
card.note: Fragrance material; skin sensitivity to essential oils is possible.

quick.overview:
Vetiver is a perennial grass whose roots are steam-distilled into a thick amber oil. In perfumery it is a staple base note: dry, woody, smoky and earthy, and common in men's fragrances. For appearance it is part of grooming, the way a person smells being one element of how they come across.

Perfumers also value it as a fixative, meaning it helps lighter notes last. Classic examples include Dior Eau Sauvage, Guerlain Vetiver and Lalique Encre Noire. Beyond fragrance, small studies have looked at vetiver aroma and attention, and at vetiver oil as a mosquito repellent.
quick.how: People wear vetiver as a cologne or eau de toilette, as one note among others or as the lead, sprayed on skin or clothes. Hair and body products sometimes carry it too. It is often compared by scent family: green and grassy, smoky, or sweet and woody.
quick.risks: Essential oils and fragrance ingredients can irritate skin or cause allergic contact reactions in some people, so patch-testing is a common precaution. Evidence for therapeutic claims such as anti-inflammatory effects comes from laboratory and review sources rather than trials in people.

lead: Vetiver, Chrysopogon zizanioides (khus), is a perennial bunchgrass of the grass family, native to India and grown across the tropics. Its deep roots stabilise soil, but its commercial value lies in the root oil.[1]

The oil is steam-distilled from dried roots, is thick and amber-brown, and smells deep, sweet, woody, smoky and earthy. It contains more than 150 identified compounds, with alpha-vetivone a key fragrant one, and is often aged for months to soften harsh notes.[1]

In perfumery vetiver is valued as a fixative and is more common in men's fragrances; examples include Dior Eau Sauvage, Guerlain Vetiver and Lalique Encre Noire.[1] People use it as a grooming scent, part of the overall impression they make.

chain: Vetiver oil anchors a fragrance base
A clean, woody, masculine scent profile
angle.text: Vetiver is worn as cologne, so its effect on appearance is through scent as part of grooming. Its fixative role is to help a fragrance linger.

paras: Worldwide production of vetiver oil is estimated at about 250 tonnes a year, with Indonesia, China and Haiti among major producers; Réunion oil, called bourbon vetiver, is often regarded as high quality. The United States, Europe, India and Japan are the main consumers.[1] Reviews describe biotechnology and biorefinery work around vetiver's volatile compounds.[3]

Perfumers use vetiver as a fixative and woody base. Reviews of the chemistry of odorants track woody and green materials in modern perfumery,[4] and a review of fragrance chemistry notes the supply challenges around woody notes.[5]
Notable vetiver fragrances include Eau Sauvage (Dior), Vétiver (Guerlain), Zizan (Ormonde Jayne), Vétiver (L'Occitane) and Encre Noire (Lalique).[1]

A review of traditional medicine describes vetiver as having a broad history of medicinal use, while noting that few published studies address disease treatment.[6] A small experiment examined volatiles from cut vetiver roots and attention during a screen task,[7] and a randomised field study compared vetiver oil with DEET as a mosquito repellent.[8] Aromatherapy reviews place essential oils among complementary strategies for mood and sleep.[9]
No clinical studies have examined vetiver fragrance for attractiveness. Trials exist on vetiver volatiles and attention[7] and on vetiver oil as a topical mosquito repellent.[8]
